items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: If you, J.C. and Bach ever swap infinite fours

ctx.x: Okay I’m trying to be like Art Tatum here, and get way, way, way off the harmonic structure of the song and find these elaborate ways to get back to it. I’m trying to do that but I am not Art Tatum. But anyway to poetry, poetry is almost antithetical to jazz in a way, especially if you write contemplative poetry as I do. I am not a performance poet. And I think the poems read well because they are basically conversational, but I don’t write for performances, a lot of contemporary poets do. There’s a generational…

I love the way you combine adjectives and nouns which — I’ll give you an example, at the end of “Dear John Coltrane” and you said, “If you, J.C. and Bach ever swap infinite fours” I just think that’s marvelous, like “infinite fours.” And it also begs the question how did you learn about the terminology that jazz musicians use all the time? The trading of fours, and the exchanges and back and forth? Was that by observing or did someone sort of take you under their wing and talk to you about that?

Well in New York I knew a lot of jazz musicians and I knew them very well. I mean that was a part of our world. The thing about the lower Manhattan arts scene in the 1960s was about as close as America ever got to say Montmartre at the turn of the 19th and 20th century, the modernism there. A great concentration of artists of all disciplines living in a relatively small area. They all knew each other, they all hung out together, they went to each other’s parties, they drank together, and the exchange was…
